doc.title: Sam Kininger interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, May 27, 2011

title: Recording, the Internet and labels
summary: Home recording, self-released label, earlier Blue Note and Sony deals, and iTunes.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Record labels, producers and the business of making albums

blocks.x: What about — things have changed very quickly now for how you record, how your records get out there, how you promote yourself. Is the Internet and YouTube and iTunes, do you think that’s been mostly a good thing?

I think so. For musicians like myself I think it has been. Because even fifteen years ago, or ten, when we first started recording the Soulive albums it had to be in a big studio, you know, like in New York or whatever, they had to be in this huge studio with a big console and everything. We don’t do anything like that now. We don’t need it. But like we recorded an album in Alan’s basement and yeah, he’s good at what he does and he’s got good equipment. He uses ProTools. But that part of it is definitely — it saves a lot of money.
And what about a record label? Do you guys do your own?

It’s our own record label now. It’s not like a SONY record deal, which we had, we had the Blue Note recording deal which was cool but getting it self-produced is definitely more advantageous to us, and like the iTunes situation is definitely good. We sold a lot of records, with Lettuce especially.
Cool. But if I went to a Barnes & Noble in Syracuse, I probably wouldn’t find Lettuce records, or would I?
You’d find Soulive ones. But people don’t even go out that much and buy CDs anywhere either.
